newsitem.title: MEXICO: Banco de Mexico assets fall, reserves rise.
newsitem.headline: Banco de Mexico assets fall, reserves rise.

text.p: Banco de Mexico said Tuesday its net international assets as of October 4 were $3.758 billion, compared with $3.864 billion on September 27.
The central bank said that its net international reserves in the same period rose to $15.833 billion from $15.571 billion.
It said the $106 million drop in international assets was due to:
-- Net revenues from operations with state oil firm Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex) of $275 million.

-- Purchases of $199 million from banks that exercised put options with the central bank sold in dollar auctions on August 30 and September 30, for amounts of $20 million and $179 million, respectively.
-- A net sale of currency to the federal government for $592 million to cover debt servicing charges.

-- A net increase of $12 million resulting from the change in dollar value of different currencies on the central bank's books, plus net returns due to interest payments and trading of metals and securities abroad, and changes in dollar bank balances at Banco de Mexico.

In the same period, the bank said, the balance of government deposits at the central bank fell 1.025 billion pesos as a result of tax revenues and outlays for the purchase of foreign exchange to service foreign debt.
During the week, credit to the bank insurance fund (Fobaproa) increased by 1.59 billion pesos.
But it said this had practically zero monetary impact because 1.469 billion pesos was deposited with withdrawal restrictions at the central bank by the bank that received the Fobaproa support.
The central bank granted credits to commercial banks for 856 million pesos chiefly to offset the monetary impact of tax collection.
The following tables detail Banco de Mexico's assets and net domestic credit. All figures are in billions of pesos, unless otherwise indicated.

*Net International Assets are defined as gross international assets minus central bank liabilities with the IMF and assets of less than a six-month duration from other central banks.
